modules.title: A. Classical mechanics
modules.doc:
Classical mechanics describes the motion of physical systems using trajectories, forces,
energies, and variational principles. Physlib develops both general formulations of the subject
and formally verified examples of mechanical systems.

## A.1. Scope

The general infrastructure includes the Euler–Lagrange equations, Hamilton's equations, and
relations between equivalent Lagrangian descriptions. Concrete models cover free particles,
harmonic and damped oscillators, pendula, rigid bodies, orbital mechanics, scattering, vibrations,
and wave equations.

## A.2. Current status

This module is an overview and currently introduces no declarations. The definitions and results
for each topic live in the corresponding submodules under `Physlib.ClassicalMechanics`.

## A.3. Future work

Shared declarations should be added here only when they apply across several areas of classical
mechanics. Definitions and results specific to one physical system should remain in its dedicated
module so that the library stays navigable.

modules.title: Configuration spaces
modules.doc:
Smooth manifolds without boundary.

## i. Overview

The configuration space of a mechanical system is the manifold of its configurations.

## ii. Key results

- `ConfigurationSpace` : a smooth manifold without boundary.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Configuration spaces

## iv. References

* V. I. Arnold, Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics. [ref: arnold_mechanics]

modules.title: Variations of curves
modules.doc:
Smooth variations of a curve in a configuration space fixing the endpoints.

## i. Overview

Variations probe the action of a Lagrangian system around a curve.

## ii. Key results

- `Variation` : smooth variations fixing the endpoints.
- `Variation.contDiff_comp_vadd` : a variation of a curve in a normed space is smooth in
  coordinates.
- `Variation.exists_bump` : a bump function gives a variation of a curve in a normed space.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Variations
- B. Variations in a normed space

## iv. References

* I. Terek, Introductory Variational Calculus on Manifolds. [ref: terek_variational_manifolds]

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.Variation
declarations.doc: A smooth variation of `γ` on `[t₀, t₁]` fixing `γ t₀` and `γ t₁`.
declarations.statement:
structure Variation (γ : Time → M) (t₀ t₁ : Time) where
  /-- The smooth family of curves. -/
  toFun : C^∞⟮𝓘(ℝ, ℝ).prod 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ), ℝ × Time; I, M⟯
  /-- Starts at `γ`. -/
  apply_zero : ∀ s ∈ Set.Icc 0 (t₁ -ᵥ t₀), toFun (0, s +ᵥ t₀) = γ (s +ᵥ t₀)
  /-- Fixes `γ t₀`. -/
  apply_left : ∀ s, toFun (s, t₀) = γ t₀
  /-- Fixes `γ t₁`. -/
  apply_right : ∀ s, toFun (s, t₁) = γ t₁

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.Variation.nonempty
declarations.doc: A smooth curve admits the constant variation.
declarations.statement:
lemma nonempty {γ : Time → M} {t₀ t₁ : Time} (hγ : ContMDiff 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ) I ∞ γ) :
    Nonempty (Variation I γ t₀ t₁)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.Variation.contDiff_comp_vadd
declarations.doc: `(s, τ) ↦ h (s, τ +ᵥ t₀)` is smooth.

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.Variation.exists_bump
declarations.doc:
For a smooth curve `γ`, smooth `ψ` supported in `(0, t₁ -ᵥ t₀)` and `w : E`, there exists a
variation `h` of `γ` with `h (s, τ +ᵥ t₀) = γ (τ +ᵥ t₀) + s • ψ τ • w`.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_bump {γ : Time → E} {t₀ t₁ : Time} (hγ : ContMDiff 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ) 𝓘(ℝ, E) ∞ γ)
    {ψ : ℝ → ℝ} (hψ : ContDiff ℝ ∞ ψ) (hs : tsupport ψ ⊆ Ioo 0 (t₁ -ᵥ t₀)) (w : E) :
    ∃ h : Variation (M := ⟨E⟩) 𝓘(ℝ, E) γ t₀ t₁,
      ∀ s τ, h.toFun (s, τ +ᵥ t₀) = γ (τ +ᵥ t₀) + s • (ψ τ • w)

modules.title: The damped harmonic oscillator
modules.doc:
The equation of motion, energy dissipation, damping regimes and variational formulation.

## i. Overview

The damped harmonic oscillator is a classical mechanical system consisting of a mass `m`
under a restoring force `- k x` and a damping force `- γ ẋ`, where `k` is the spring
constant, `γ` is the damping coefficient, `x` is the position, and `ẋ` is the velocity.

The equation of motion for the damped harmonic oscillator is:
```
m ẍ + γ ẋ + k x = 0
```

Depending on the relationship between the damping coefficient and the natural frequency,
the system exhibits three different behaviors:
- **Underdamped** (`γ^2 < 4 * m * k`) : oscillatory motion with exponentially decaying
  amplitude.
- **Critically damped** (`γ^2 = 4 * m * k`) : fastest return to equilibrium without
  oscillation.
- **Overdamped** (`4 * m * k < γ^2`) : slow return to equilibrium without oscillation.

In this file, the position and velocity both have type `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)`. This
coordinate model is useful for a first formalization, but it works only because the
one-dimensional configuration space and its tangent space are both isomorphic to
one-dimensional Euclidean space. A more geometric formalization should represent the
configuration space and its tangent bundle directly.

## ii. Key results

The key results in the study of the classical damped harmonic oscillator are the following:

In the `Basic` module:
- `DampedHarmonicOscillator` contains the input data to the problem.
- `EquationOfMotion` defines the damped oscillator equation `m ẍ + γ ẋ + k x = 0`.
- `energy_dissipation_rate` computes the rate at which damping removes mechanical energy.
- `energy_balance` gives the mechanical energy change over a finite time interval.
- `energy_antitone` shows that mechanical energy is nonincreasing along a solution.
- `IsUnderdamped`, `IsCriticallyDamped`, and `IsOverdamped` define the three damping
  regimes from the discriminant `γ^2 - 4 * m * k`.
- `angularFrequency` selects the real frequency parameter from the damping regime.
- `qualityFactor` and `relaxationTime` define the quality factor `Q = ω / (2 β)` and the
  amplitude relaxation time `τ = 1 / β` from the decay rate `β = γ / (2 m)`;
  `isUnderdamped_iff_half_lt_qualityFactor` and its companions characterise the three damping
  regimes by `Q`.
- `toUndamped_equationOfMotion` relates the damped and undamped equations of motion when
  the damping coefficient is zero.
- `lagrangian` defines the Caldirola–Kanai lagrangian `exp (γ/m * t) * (T - V)`.
- `gradLagrangian` defines the variational gradient of the corresponding action, and
  `equationOfMotion_iff_gradLagrangian_zero` shows that its vanishing is equivalent to
  the equation of motion.

In the `Solution` module:
- `InitialConditions` contains the initial position and velocity.
- `trajectory` gives the explicit solution selected from the damping regime.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The input data
- B. The equation of motion and energy dissipation
  - B.1. The equation of motion
  - B.2. Energy dissipation
- C. Newton's second law
  - C.1. The force
  - C.2. Equation of motion if and only if Newton's second law
- D. Damping regimes
  - D.1. The discriminant, the decay rate and the angular frequency
  - D.2. The quality factor and the relaxation time
- E. To undamped oscillator
- F. The Caldirola–Kanai lagrangian and the equation of motion
  - F.1. The lagrangian
    - F.1.1. Equalities for the lagrangian
    - F.1.2. Smoothness of the lagrangian
    - F.1.3. Gradients of the lagrangian
  - F.2. The variational gradient of the action
    - F.2.1. The variational gradient and Newton's second law
  - F.3. Equation of motion iff the variational gradient vanishes

## iv. References

References for the damped harmonic oscillator include:

* Landau & Lifshitz, Mechanics, page 76, section 25. [ref: landau_mechanics]
* Goldstein, Classical Mechanics, Chapter 6, Section 6.5 (Forced Vibrations and the Effect of
  Dissipative Forces). [ref: goldstein_classicalmechanics]

References for the Caldirola–Kanai lagrangian include:

* Caldirola, Nuovo Cimento 18 (1941) 393. [ref: caldirola_1941]
* Kanai, Progress of Theoretical Physics 3 (1948) 440. [ref: kanai_1948]

sections.text:
## A. The input data

We start by defining a structure containing the input data of the damped harmonic oscillator.
The mass `m` and spring constant `k` are inherited from `HarmonicOscillator`; this file adds
the damping coefficient `γ`.

The mass/spring nonzero lemmas, the natural angular frequency, and the undamped energy API
are inherited from `HarmonicOscillator`.

## B. The equation of motion and energy dissipation

### B.1. The equation of motion

### B.2. Energy dissipation

The damped oscillator inherits the mechanical energy from the undamped harmonic oscillator.
Along a solution of the damped equation of motion, that energy decreases at a rate
proportional to `-γ ‖ẋ‖^2`.

## C. Newton's second law

We define the force of the damped oscillator, and show that the equation of
motion is equivalent to Newton's second law.

### C.1. The force

We define the force of the damped oscillator as `- k x - γ v`.

### C.2. Equation of motion if and only if Newton's second law

We show that the equation of motion is equivalent to Newton's second law.

## D. Damping regimes

The sign of the discriminant `γ^2 - 4 * m * k` separates the underdamped, critically
damped, and overdamped regimes. We also define the decay rate and the regime-selected
real frequency that appears in the explicit solution formulas.
### D.1. The discriminant, the decay rate and the angular frequency

### D.2. The quality factor and the relaxation time

The quality factor `Q = ω / (2 β)` and the amplitude relaxation time `τ = 1 / β` are the
usual dimensionless and dimensionful measures of the damping, both expressed through the
decay rate `β = γ / (2 m)`. When `γ = 0` both are `0` by the convention `x / 0 = 0` of Lean,
so the lemmas below assume `0 < γ` whenever the value matters.

## E. To undamped oscillator

We show that the damped harmonic oscillator reduces to the undamped harmonic oscillator when the
damping coefficient is zero. The underlying mass and spring data are already inherited from
`HarmonicOscillator`; the proof argument records that this conversion is being used only in
the zero-damping case.

We also show that the equations of motion are equivalent in this case.

## F. The Caldirola–Kanai lagrangian and the equation of motion

The damped harmonic oscillator is not conservative, so the undamped lagrangian
`T - V` does not reproduce the damped equation of motion. Instead we use the
Caldirola–Kanai lagrangian, which multiplies the undamped lagrangian by the
time-dependent factor `exp (γ/m * t)`:

$$L(t, x, v) = e^{(\gamma/m) t}\left(\frac{1}{2} m \|v\|^2 - \frac{1}{2} k \|x\|^2\right)$$

Setting the variational gradient of the corresponding action equal to zero
recovers exactly the damped equation of motion `m ẍ + γ ẋ + k x = 0`.

### F.1. The lagrangian

We define the Caldirola–Kanai lagrangian as the lagrangian of the underlying
undamped harmonic oscillator multiplied by the exponential factor `exp (γ/m * t)`.

#### F.1.1. Equalities for the lagrangian

We prove some simple equalities for the lagrangian, in particular that when applied to a
trajectory it is the exponential factor times the kinetic energy minus the potential energy,
and that it reduces to the undamped lagrangian when the damping coefficient is zero.

#### F.1.2. Smoothness of the lagrangian

The lagrangian is smooth in all its arguments.

#### F.1.3. Gradients of the lagrangian

We now show results related to the gradients of the lagrangian with respect to the
position and velocity. They follow from the corresponding gradients of the undamped
lagrangian, using that the gradient scales with the constant `exp (γ/m * t)`.

### F.2. The variational gradient of the action

We now write down the variational gradient of the action of the damped harmonic
oscillator, for a trajectory $x(t)$ this is equal to

$$t\mapsto \left.\frac{\partial L(t, q, \dot x (t))}{\partial q}\right|_{q = x(t)} -
  \frac{d}{dt} \left.\frac{\partial L(t, x(t), v)}{\partial v}\right|_{v = \dot x (t)}$$

Setting this equal to zero corresponds to the Euler-Lagrange equations, and thereby the
equation of motion.

#### F.2.1. The variational gradient and Newton's second law

We simplify the variational gradient of the action to the exponential factor times
the difference between the force and mass times acceleration.

### F.3. Equation of motion iff the variational gradient vanishes

The equation of motion of the damped harmonic oscillator holds if and only if the
variational gradient of the Caldirola–Kanai action vanishes, since the exponential
factor is never zero.

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator
declarations.doc:
The classical damped harmonic oscillator is specified by a mass `m`, a spring
constant `k`, and a damping coefficient `γ`.

The mass and spring constant are inherited from `HarmonicOscillator` and are positive.
The damping coefficient is assumed to be nonnegative.
declarations.statement:
structure DampedHarmonicOscillator extends HarmonicOscillator where
  /-- The damping coefficient of the oscillator. -/
  γ : ℝ
  /-- The damping coefficient is nonnegative. -/
  γ_nonneg : 0 ≤ γ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.EquationOfMotion
declarations.doc:
The equation of motion for the damped harmonic oscillator:
`m ẍ + γ ẋ + k x = 0`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def EquationOfMotion (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.acceleration_eq_of_equationOfMotion
declarations.doc:
Solving the equation of motion for the acceleration: along a solution the second derivative
is `-(k/m) x - (γ/m) ẋ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma acceleration_eq_of_equationOfMotion (z : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1))
    (hEOM : S.EquationOfMotion z) (t : Time) :
    ∂ₜ (∂ₜ z) t = (-(S.m⁻¹ * S.k)) • z t + (-(S.m⁻¹ * S.γ)) • ∂ₜ z t

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.energy_dissipation_rate
declarations.doc:
Along a smooth solution of the damped equation of motion, the derivative of the
mechanical energy is `-γ ‖ẋ‖^2`.
declarations.statement:
lemma energy_dissipation_rate (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) (t : Time)
    (h1 : S.EquationOfMotion xₜ)
    (hx : ContDiff ℝ ∞ xₜ) :
    ∂ₜ (S.energy xₜ) t = - S.γ * ⟪∂ₜ xₜ t, ∂ₜ xₜ t⟫_ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.energy_not_conserved
declarations.doc:
If `0 < γ` and the velocity is nonzero at a time, the mechanical energy is strictly
decreasing at that time.
declarations.statement:
lemma energy_not_conserved (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) (t : Time)
    (h1 : S.EquationOfMotion xₜ) (hx : ContDiff ℝ ∞ xₜ) (hdx : ∂ₜ xₜ t ≠ 0) (hγ : 0 < S.γ) :
    ∂ₜ (S.energy xₜ) t < 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.energy_balance
declarations.doc:
The mechanical energy change between two times equals the work done by damping.
The interval integral is oriented, so the identity holds in either time order.
declarations.statement:
lemma energy_balance (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1))
    (hEOM : S.EquationOfMotion xₜ) (hx : ContDiff ℝ ∞ xₜ) (a b : ℝ) :
    S.energy xₜ ⟨b⟩ - S.energy xₜ ⟨a⟩ =
      -S.γ * ∫ t in a..b, ‖∂ₜ xₜ ⟨t⟩‖ ^ 2

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.energy_antitone
declarations.doc: Mechanical energy is nonincreasing along every smooth solution, including zero damping.
declarations.statement:
lemma energy_antitone (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1))
    (hEOM : S.EquationOfMotion xₜ) (hx : ContDiff ℝ ∞ xₜ) :
    Antitone (fun t : ℝ => S.energy xₜ ⟨t⟩)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.energy_le_initial
declarations.doc: At nonnegative times the mechanical energy is bounded by its initial value.
declarations.statement:
lemma energy_le_initial (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1))
    (hEOM : S.EquationOfMotion xₜ) (hx : ContDiff ℝ ∞ xₜ) (t : Time) (ht : 0 ≤ t.val) :
    S.energy xₜ t ≤ S.energy xₜ 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.force
declarations.doc: The force of the damped harmonic oscillator at a given position and time.
declarations.statement:
noncomputable def force (S : DampedHarmonicOscillator)
    (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) (t : Time) :
    EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.equationOfMotion_iff_newtons_2nd_law
declarations.statement:
lemma equationOfMotion_iff_newtons_2nd_law (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) :
    S.EquationOfMotion xₜ ↔
    (∀ t : Time, S.m • ∂ₜ (∂ₜ xₜ) t = force S xₜ t)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.discriminant
declarations.doc: The discriminant that determines the damping regime.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def discriminant : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.decayRate
declarations.doc: The exponential decay rate `γ / (2 * m)`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def decayRate : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.IsUnderdamped
declarations.doc: The system is underdamped when γ² < 4mk.
declarations.statement: def IsUnderdamped : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.IsCriticallyDamped
declarations.doc: The system is critically damped when γ² = 4mk.
declarations.statement: def IsCriticallyDamped : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.IsOverdamped
declarations.doc: The system is overdamped when 4mk < γ².
declarations.statement: def IsOverdamped : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.isUnderdamped_or_isCriticallyDamped_or_isOverdamped
declarations.doc: Every damped oscillator is underdamped, critically damped, or overdamped.
declarations.statement:
lemma isUnderdamped_or_isCriticallyDamped_or_isOverdamped :
    S.IsUnderdamped ∨ S.IsCriticallyDamped ∨ S.IsOverdamped

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.IsUndamped
declarations.doc: The system is undamped when γ = 0.
declarations.statement: def IsUndamped : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.angularFrequency
declarations.doc:
The real frequency selected by the damping regime.

In the underdamped regime this is the oscillation frequency. In the critically damped
regime it is `0`. In the overdamped regime this is the real split rate between the two
roots.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def angularFrequency : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.discriminant_eq_four_mul_m_sq_mul_decayRate_sq_sub_ω_sq
declarations.doc: The relationship between the discriminant, decay rate, and natural angular frequency.
declarations.statement:
lemma discriminant_eq_four_mul_m_sq_mul_decayRate_sq_sub_ω_sq :
    S.discriminant = 4 * S.m^2 * (S.decayRate^2 - S.ω^2)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.decayRate_nonneg
declarations.doc: The decay rate is nonnegative.
declarations.statement: lemma decayRate_nonneg : 0 ≤ S.decayRate

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.decayRate_pos
declarations.doc: The decay rate is positive when the damping coefficient is positive.
declarations.statement: lemma decayRate_pos (hγ : 0 < S.γ) : 0 < S.decayRate

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.isUnderdamped_of_gamma_eq_zero
declarations.doc: An undamped oscillator lies in the underdamped regime.
declarations.statement: lemma isUnderdamped_of_gamma_eq_zero (hγ : S.γ = 0) : S.IsUnderdamped

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.isUnderdamped_decayRate
declarations.doc: An underdamped system has decay rate less than the natural frequency.
declarations.statement: lemma isUnderdamped_decayRate (hS : S.IsUnderdamped) : S.decayRate < S.ω

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.isCriticallyDamped_decayRate
declarations.doc: A critically damped system has decay rate equal to the natural frequency.
declarations.statement: lemma isCriticallyDamped_decayRate (hS : S.IsCriticallyDamped) : S.ω = S.decayRate

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.gamma_eq_two_mul_m_mul_decayRate
declarations.doc: The damping coefficient is twice mass times the decay rate.
declarations.statement: lemma gamma_eq_two_mul_m_mul_decayRate : S.γ = 2 * S.m * S.decayRate

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.k_eq_m_mul_ω_sq
declarations.doc: The spring constant is `m * ω^2`.
declarations.statement: lemma k_eq_m_mul_ω_sq : S.k = S.m * S.ω^2

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.k_eq_m_mul_decayRate_sq_of_criticallyDamped
declarations.doc: In the critically damped regime, `k = m * decayRate^2`.
declarations.statement:
lemma k_eq_m_mul_decayRate_sq_of_criticallyDamped (hS : S.IsCriticallyDamped) :
    S.k = S.m * S.decayRate^2

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.isOverdamped_decayRate
declarations.doc: An overdamped system has decay rate greater than the natural frequency.
declarations.statement: lemma isOverdamped_decayRate (hS : S.IsOverdamped) : S.ω < S.decayRate

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.angularFrequency_eq_underdamped
declarations.doc: In the underdamped regime, the selected frequency uses the oscillation frequency.
declarations.statement:
lemma angularFrequency_eq_underdamped (hS : S.IsUnderdamped) :
    S.angularFrequency = sqrt (- S.discriminant) / (2 * S.m)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.angularFrequency_eq_criticallyDamped
declarations.doc: In the critically damped regime, the selected frequency is zero.
declarations.statement:
lemma angularFrequency_eq_criticallyDamped (hS : S.IsCriticallyDamped) :
    S.angularFrequency = 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.angularFrequency_eq_overdamped
declarations.doc: In the overdamped regime, the selected frequency uses the real split rate.
declarations.statement:
lemma angularFrequency_eq_overdamped (hS : S.IsOverdamped) :
    S.angularFrequency = sqrt S.discriminant / (2 * S.m)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.angularFrequency_sq_of_underdamped
declarations.doc:
In the underdamped regime, the selected angular frequency squares to
`ω^2 - decayRate^2`.
declarations.statement:
lemma angularFrequency_sq_of_underdamped (hS : S.IsUnderdamped) :
    S.angularFrequency^2 = S.ω^2 - S.decayRate^2

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.angularFrequency_pos_of_underdamped
declarations.doc: The selected angular frequency is positive in the underdamped regime.
declarations.statement:
lemma angularFrequency_pos_of_underdamped (hS : S.IsUnderdamped) :
    0 < S.angularFrequency

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.angularFrequency_ne_zero_of_underdamped
declarations.doc: The selected angular frequency is nonzero in the underdamped regime.
declarations.statement:
lemma angularFrequency_ne_zero_of_underdamped (hS : S.IsUnderdamped) :
    S.angularFrequency ≠ 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.angularFrequency_sq_of_overdamped
declarations.doc:
In the overdamped regime, the selected angular frequency squares to
`decayRate^2 - ω^2`.
declarations.statement:
lemma angularFrequency_sq_of_overdamped (hS : S.IsOverdamped) :
    S.angularFrequency^2 = S.decayRate^2 - S.ω^2

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.angularFrequency_pos_of_overdamped
declarations.doc: The selected angular frequency is positive in the overdamped regime.
declarations.statement:
lemma angularFrequency_pos_of_overdamped (hS : S.IsOverdamped) :
    0 < S.angularFrequency

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.angularFrequency_ne_zero_of_overdamped
declarations.doc: The selected angular frequency is nonzero in the overdamped regime.
declarations.statement:
lemma angularFrequency_ne_zero_of_overdamped (hS : S.IsOverdamped) :
    S.angularFrequency ≠ 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.isUnderdamped_iff_decayRate_lt
declarations.doc: The underdamped regime is characterised by `β < ω`.
declarations.statement: lemma isUnderdamped_iff_decayRate_lt : S.IsUnderdamped ↔ S.decayRate < S.ω

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.isCriticallyDamped_iff_eq_decayRate
declarations.doc: The critically damped regime is characterised by `ω = β`.
declarations.statement: lemma isCriticallyDamped_iff_eq_decayRate : S.IsCriticallyDamped ↔ S.ω = S.decayRate

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.isOverdamped_iff_lt_decayRate
declarations.doc: The overdamped regime is characterised by `ω < β`.
declarations.statement: lemma isOverdamped_iff_lt_decayRate : S.IsOverdamped ↔ S.ω < S.decayRate

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.qualityFactor
declarations.doc:
The quality factor `Q = ω / (2 β)`, equal to `m ω / γ` and to `√(m k) / γ`: the ratio of
the natural angular frequency to the width `γ / m` of the resonance.

When `γ = 0` the value is `0` by the convention `x / 0 = 0`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def qualityFactor : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.relaxationTime
declarations.doc:
The relaxation time `τ = 1 / β` of the amplitude, equal to `2 m / γ`; the exponential
factor of the solutions is `exp (-t / τ)` (see `exp_neg_decayRate_mul`).

When `γ = 0` the value is `0` by the convention `0⁻¹ = 0`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def relaxationTime : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.qualityFactor_eq_m_mul_ω_div_γ
declarations.doc: The quality factor equals `m ω / γ`.
declarations.statement: lemma qualityFactor_eq_m_mul_ω_div_γ : S.qualityFactor = S.m * S.ω / S.γ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.qualityFactor_eq_sqrt_div
declarations.doc: The quality factor equals `√(m k) / γ`.
declarations.statement: lemma qualityFactor_eq_sqrt_div : S.qualityFactor = √(S.m * S.k) / S.γ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.qualityFactor_pos
declarations.doc: The quality factor is positive when the damping coefficient is positive.
declarations.statement: lemma qualityFactor_pos (hγ : 0 < S.γ) : 0 < S.qualityFactor

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.qualityFactor_sq
declarations.doc: The square of the quality factor equals `m k / γ ^ 2`.
declarations.statement: lemma qualityFactor_sq : S.qualityFactor ^ 2 = S.m * S.k / S.γ ^ 2

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.discriminant_eq_mul_qualityFactor
declarations.doc:
The discriminant in terms of the quality factor: `γ ^ 2 - 4 m k = 4 m k (1 / (4 Q ^ 2) - 1)`;
for `γ = 0` both sides equal `-4 m k`.
declarations.statement:
lemma discriminant_eq_mul_qualityFactor :
    S.discriminant = 4 * S.m * S.k * (1 / (4 * S.qualityFactor ^ 2) - 1)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.isUnderdamped_iff_half_lt_qualityFactor
declarations.doc: The underdamped regime is characterised by `1 / 2 < Q` when `0 < γ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma isUnderdamped_iff_half_lt_qualityFactor (hγ : 0 < S.γ) :
    S.IsUnderdamped ↔ 1 / 2 < S.qualityFactor

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.isCriticallyDamped_iff_qualityFactor_eq_half
declarations.doc: The critically damped regime is characterised by `Q = 1 / 2` when `0 < γ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma isCriticallyDamped_iff_qualityFactor_eq_half (hγ : 0 < S.γ) :
    S.IsCriticallyDamped ↔ S.qualityFactor = 1 / 2

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.isOverdamped_iff_qualityFactor_lt_half
declarations.doc: The overdamped regime is characterised by `Q < 1 / 2` when `0 < γ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma isOverdamped_iff_qualityFactor_lt_half (hγ : 0 < S.γ) :
    S.IsOverdamped ↔ S.qualityFactor < 1 / 2

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.angularFrequency_sq_eq_mul_qualityFactor
declarations.doc:
In the underdamped regime the selected angular frequency satisfies
`ω_d ^ 2 = ω ^ 2 (1 - 1 / (4 Q ^ 2))` when `0 < γ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma angularFrequency_sq_eq_mul_qualityFactor (hγ : 0 < S.γ) (hS : S.IsUnderdamped) :
    S.angularFrequency ^ 2 = S.ω ^ 2 * (1 - 1 / (4 * S.qualityFactor ^ 2))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.relaxationTime_eq
declarations.doc: The relaxation time equals `2 m / γ`.
declarations.statement: lemma relaxationTime_eq : S.relaxationTime = 2 * S.m / S.γ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.decayRate_mul_relaxationTime
declarations.doc: The decay rate and the relaxation time are inverse to each other when `0 < γ`.
declarations.statement: lemma decayRate_mul_relaxationTime (hγ : 0 < S.γ) : S.decayRate * S.relaxationTime = 1

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.relaxationTime_pos
declarations.doc: The relaxation time is positive when the damping coefficient is positive.
declarations.statement: lemma relaxationTime_pos (hγ : 0 < S.γ) : 0 < S.relaxationTime

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.qualityFactor_eq_ω_mul_relaxationTime
declarations.doc: The quality factor equals `ω τ / 2`; this holds for `γ = 0` as well, both sides being `0`.
declarations.statement: lemma qualityFactor_eq_ω_mul_relaxationTime : S.qualityFactor = S.ω * S.relaxationTime / 2

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.exp_neg_decayRate_mul
declarations.doc:
The exponential factor `exp (-β t)` of the solutions equals `exp (-t / τ)`; for `γ = 0`
both sides equal `1`.
declarations.statement:
lemma exp_neg_decayRate_mul (t : Time) :
    exp (-S.decayRate * t) = exp (-(t : ℝ) / S.relaxationTime)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.toUndamped
declarations.doc: Convert a damped oscillator to its underlying undamped oscillator when `γ = 0`.
declarations.statement:
def toUndamped (S : DampedHarmonicOscillator) (_hS : S.IsUndamped) :
    HarmonicOscillator

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.toUndamped_equationOfMotion
declarations.doc:
When `γ = 0`, the damped equation of motion is equivalent to the equation of motion
for the corresponding undamped harmonic oscillator.
declarations.statement:
lemma toUndamped_equationOfMotion (S : DampedHarmonicOscillator) (hS : S.IsUndamped)
    (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) (hx : ContDiff ℝ ∞ xₜ) :
    S.EquationOfMotion xₜ ↔ (S.toUndamped hS).EquationOfMotion xₜ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.lagrangian
declarations.doc:
The Caldirola–Kanai lagrangian of the damped harmonic oscillator. It is the
lagrangian of the underlying undamped harmonic oscillator multiplied by the
time-dependent factor `exp (γ/m * t)`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def lagrangian (t : Time) (x v : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.lagrangian_eq
declarations.statement:
lemma lagrangian_eq : S.lagrangian = fun (t : Time) (x v : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) =>
    exp (S.γ / S.m * t) * (1 / (2 : ℝ) * S.m * ⟪v, v⟫_ℝ - 1 / (2 : ℝ) * S.k * ⟪x, x⟫_ℝ)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.lagrangian_eq_exp_mul_kineticEnergy_sub_potentialEnergy
declarations.statement:
lemma lagrangian_eq_exp_mul_kineticEnergy_sub_potentialEnergy (t : Time)
    (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) :
    S.lagrangian t (xₜ t) (∂ₜ xₜ t) =
      exp (S.γ / S.m * t) * (S.kineticEnergy xₜ t - S.potentialEnergy (xₜ t))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.lagrangian_of_isUndamped
declarations.doc:
When the damping coefficient is zero, the Caldirola–Kanai lagrangian is the
lagrangian of the underlying undamped harmonic oscillator.
declarations.statement:
lemma lagrangian_of_isUndamped (hS : S.IsUndamped) :
    S.lagrangian = S.toHarmonicOscillator.lagrangian

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.contDiff_lagrangian
declarations.statement: lemma contDiff_lagrangian (n : WithTop ℕ∞) : ContDiff ℝ n ↿S.lagrangian

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.gradient_lagrangian_position_eq
declarations.statement:
lemma gradient_lagrangian_position_eq (t : Time) (x v : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) :
    gradient (fun x => S.lagrangian t x v) x = -(exp (S.γ / S.m * t) * S.k) • x

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.gradient_lagrangian_velocity_eq
declarations.statement:
lemma gradient_lagrangian_velocity_eq (t : Time) (x v : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) :
    gradient (S.lagrangian t x) v = (exp (S.γ / S.m * t) * S.m) • v

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.gradLagrangian
declarations.doc: The variational gradient of the action of the damped harmonic oscillator.
declarations.statement:
noncomputable def gradLagrangian (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) :
    Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.gradLagrangian_eq_eulerLagrangeOp
declarations.statement:
lemma gradLagrangian_eq_eulerLagrangeOp (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1))
    (hq : ContDiff ℝ ∞ xₜ) :
    S.gradLagrangian xₜ = eulerLagrangeOp S.lagrangian xₜ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.gradLagrangian_eq_force
declarations.doc:
The variational gradient of the Caldirola–Kanai action is the exponential factor
times the difference of the force and mass times acceleration appearing in
Newton's second law.
declarations.statement:
lemma gradLagrangian_eq_force (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)) (hx : ContDiff ℝ ∞ xₜ) :
    S.gradLagrangian xₜ = fun t : Time =>
      exp (S.γ / S.m * t) • (force S xₜ t - S.m • ∂ₜ (∂ₜ xₜ) t)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.equationOfMotion_iff_gradLagrangian_zero
declarations.statement:
lemma equationOfMotion_iff_gradLagrangian_zero (xₜ : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1))
    (hx : ContDiff ℝ ∞ xₜ) :
    S.EquationOfMotion xₜ ↔ S.gradLagrangian xₜ = 0

modules.title: Solutions to the damped harmonic oscillator
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

In this module we define the solution to the damped harmonic oscillator for given initial
conditions and prove that it satisfies the equation of motion. The solution selects the
appropriate closed form from the sign of the discriminant: trigonometric for the underdamped
case, polynomial for the critically damped case, and hyperbolic for the overdamped case.

## ii. Key results

- `InitialConditions` is a structure for the initial position and velocity.
- `trajectory` selects the appropriate regime-specific trajectory from the sign of the
  discriminant; `trajectory_eq_of_underdamped_relaxationTime` rewrites the underdamped
  solution with the relaxation time `τ`.
- `trajectory_equationOfMotion_of_underdamped`,
  `trajectory_equationOfMotion_of_criticallyDamped`, and
  `trajectory_equationOfMotion_of_overdamped` prove the selected trajectory satisfies the
  equation of motion in each damping regime.
- `trajectory_equationOfMotion` proves that the selected trajectory satisfies the equation
  of motion.
- `equationOfMotion_unique` proves that two smooth solutions with the same initial data agree, and
  `trajectories_unique` proves that the selected trajectory is the unique solution with the given
  initial conditions.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The initial conditions
- B. Trajectories associated with the initial conditions
  - B.1. Regime-specific base trajectories
  - B.2. The selected trajectory
  - B.3. Shared calculus lemmas
  - B.4. Derivatives of the base trajectories
- C. Trajectories and equation of motion
  - C.1. The selected trajectory satisfies the equation of motion
  - C.2. Uniqueness of the solutions

## iv. References

References for the damped harmonic oscillator include:

* Landau & Lifshitz, Mechanics, page 76, section 25. [ref: landau_mechanics]
* Goldstein, Classical Mechanics, Chapter 6, Section 6.5 (Forced Vibrations and the Effect of
  Dissipative Forces). [ref: goldstein_classicalmechanics]

sections.text:
## A. The initial conditions

We define the type of initial conditions for the damped harmonic oscillator. The initial
conditions are the position and velocity at time `0`.

## B. Trajectories associated with the initial conditions

For each damping regime, we give an explicit formula for the trajectory with the specified
initial conditions.

### B.1. Regime-specific base trajectories
### B.2. The selected trajectory

### B.3. Shared calculus lemmas

The three solution formulas all have the form `exp (-a * t) • y t`. The following private
lemmas compute the first and second derivatives of that expression and package the common
equation-of-motion argument.

### B.4. Derivatives of the base trajectories

The remaining private lemmas compute the velocity and acceleration of the trigonometric,
polynomial, and hyperbolic base trajectories before the exponential decay factor is applied.

## C. Trajectories and equation of motion

The regime-specific trajectories satisfy the equation of motion for the damped harmonic
oscillator.

### C.1. The selected trajectory satisfies the equation of motion

### C.2. Uniqueness of the solutions

Unlike the undamped oscillator, the mechanical energy is not conserved along a damped solution, so
uniqueness cannot be read off from a conserved positive-definite energy. Instead we reduce the
second-order equation of motion `m ẍ + γ ẋ + k x = 0` to the first-order linear system
`(x, ẋ)' = (ẋ, (1/m)(-k x - γ ẋ))` on the phase space and invoke the global
ODE-uniqueness theorem `ODE_solution_unique_univ` (the right-hand side is a continuous
linear map, hence Lipschitz).

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.InitialConditions
declarations.doc:
The initial conditions for the damped harmonic oscillator, specified by an initial
position and an initial velocity.
declarations.statement:
structure InitialConditions where
  /-- The initial position of the damped harmonic oscillator. -/
  x₀ : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)
  /-- The initial velocity of the damped harmonic oscillator. -/
  v₀ : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.underdampedBase
declarations.doc: The oscillatory part of the underdamped trajectory before exponential decay.
declarations.statement:
noncomputable def underdampedBase
    (IC : InitialConditions) : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.criticallyDampedBase
declarations.doc: The polynomial part of the critically damped trajectory before exponential decay.
declarations.statement:
noncomputable def criticallyDampedBase
    (IC : InitialConditions) : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.overdampedBase
declarations.doc: The hyperbolic part of the overdamped trajectory before exponential decay.
declarations.statement:
noncomputable def overdampedBase
    (IC : InitialConditions) : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.trajectory
declarations.doc:
Given initial conditions, the solution selected from the damping regime of the
oscillator.
declarations.statement:
noncomputable def trajectory
    (IC : InitialConditions) : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.trajectory_eq_of_underdamped
declarations.doc: In the underdamped regime, the selected trajectory uses the trigonometric base.
declarations.statement:
lemma trajectory_eq_of_underdamped (IC : InitialConditions) (hS : S.IsUnderdamped) :
    S.trajectory IC =
      fun t : Time => exp (-S.decayRate * t) • S.underdampedBase IC t

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.trajectory_eq_of_criticallyDamped
declarations.doc: In the critically damped regime, the selected trajectory uses the polynomial base.
declarations.statement:
lemma trajectory_eq_of_criticallyDamped (IC : InitialConditions) (hS : S.IsCriticallyDamped) :
    S.trajectory IC =
      fun t : Time => exp (-S.decayRate * t) • S.criticallyDampedBase IC t

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.trajectory_eq_of_overdamped
declarations.doc: In the overdamped regime, the selected trajectory uses the hyperbolic base.
declarations.statement:
lemma trajectory_eq_of_overdamped (IC : InitialConditions) (hS : S.IsOverdamped) :
    S.trajectory IC =
      fun t : Time => exp (-S.decayRate * t) • S.overdampedBase IC t

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.trajectory_eq_of_underdamped_relaxationTime
declarations.doc:
In the underdamped regime, the selected trajectory is `exp (-t / τ)` times the
trigonometric base, `τ` being the relaxation time.
declarations.statement:
lemma trajectory_eq_of_underdamped_relaxationTime (IC : InitialConditions)
    (hS : S.IsUnderdamped) :
    S.trajectory IC =
      fun t : Time => exp (-(t : ℝ) / S.relaxationTime) • S.underdampedBase IC t

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.trajectory_contDiff
declarations.doc: The selected trajectory is smooth.
declarations.statement:
lemma trajectory_contDiff (IC : InitialConditions) :
    ContDiff ℝ ∞ (S.trajectory IC)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.trajectory_apply_zero
declarations.doc: The selected trajectory has initial position `IC.x₀`.
declarations.statement: lemma trajectory_apply_zero (IC : InitialConditions) : S.trajectory IC 0 = IC.x₀

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.trajectory_velocity_at_zero
declarations.doc: The selected trajectory has initial velocity `IC.v₀`.
declarations.statement:
lemma trajectory_velocity_at_zero (IC : InitialConditions) :
    ∂ₜ (S.trajectory IC) 0 = IC.v₀

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.trajectory_equationOfMotion_of_criticallyDamped
declarations.doc:
In the critically damped regime, the selected trajectory satisfies the damped equation
of motion.
declarations.statement:
lemma trajectory_equationOfMotion_of_criticallyDamped (IC : InitialConditions)
    (hS : S.IsCriticallyDamped) :
    S.EquationOfMotion (S.trajectory IC)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.trajectory_equationOfMotion_of_underdamped
declarations.doc:
In the underdamped regime, the selected trajectory satisfies the damped equation of
motion.
declarations.statement:
lemma trajectory_equationOfMotion_of_underdamped (IC : InitialConditions)
    (hS : S.IsUnderdamped) :
    S.EquationOfMotion (S.trajectory IC)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.trajectory_equationOfMotion_of_overdamped
declarations.doc:
In the overdamped regime, the selected trajectory satisfies the damped equation of
motion.
declarations.statement:
lemma trajectory_equationOfMotion_of_overdamped (IC : InitialConditions)
    (hS : S.IsOverdamped) :
    S.EquationOfMotion (S.trajectory IC)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.trajectory_equationOfMotion
declarations.doc: The selected trajectory satisfies the damped equation of motion.
declarations.statement:
lemma trajectory_equationOfMotion (IC : InitialConditions) :
    S.EquationOfMotion (S.trajectory IC)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.equationOfMotion_unique
declarations.doc:
Any two smooth solutions of the damped equation of motion with the same initial position and
velocity are equal.
declarations.statement:
lemma equationOfMotion_unique (x y : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1))
    (hx : ContDiff ℝ ∞ x) (hy : ContDiff ℝ ∞ y)
    (hEOMx : S.EquationOfMotion x) (hEOMy : S.EquationOfMotion y)
    (h0 : x 0 = y 0) (hv0 : ∂ₜ x 0 = ∂ₜ y 0) :
    x = y

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.DampedHarmonicOscillator.trajectories_unique
declarations.doc:
The selected trajectory is the unique smooth solution of the damped equation of motion with the
given initial conditions.
declarations.statement:
lemma trajectories_unique (IC : InitialConditions) (x : Time → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1))
    (hx : ContDiff ℝ ∞ x) (hEOM : S.EquationOfMotion x)
    (hx0 : x 0 = IC.x₀) (hv0 : ∂ₜ x 0 = IC.v₀) :
    x = S.trajectory IC

modules.title: A. Euler–Lagrange equations
modules.doc:
The Euler–Lagrange equations characterize stationary trajectories of an action functional. For a
Lagrangian `L t q v`, they compare the gradient with respect to position to the time derivative of
the gradient with respect to velocity.

## A.1. Mathematical setting

Trajectories take values in a complete real inner-product space `X`. The Lagrangian has type
`Time → X → X → ℝ`, and the corresponding action is the time integral of
`L t (q t) (∂ₜ q t)`.

## A.2. Main definitions and results

- `eulerLagrangeOp` defines the Euler–Lagrange operator
  `∂L/∂q - ∂ₜ (∂L/∂v)` along a trajectory.
- `eulerLagrangeOp_eq` exposes its pointwise formula.
- `eulerLagrangeOp_zero` evaluates the operator for the zero Lagrangian.
- `euler_lagrange_varGradient` proves that the variational gradient of the action equals the
  Euler–Lagrange operator for smooth trajectories and Lagrangians.
- `canonicalMomentum` and `eulerLagrange` give the covector form `∂L/∂q - dₜ(∂L/∂q̇)` for a
  Lagrangian system `S` on a normed space `E` and time origin `t₀`, with `contDiff_eulerLagrange`,
  `eulerLagrange_congr` and `eulerLagrange_congr_lagrangian`.

## A.3. Current scope

The result is formulated for smooth data and Hilbert-space-valued trajectories. Applications to
specific mechanical systems are developed in their corresponding modules, where vanishing of the
operator becomes the system's equation of motion.

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.eulerLagrangeOp
declarations.doc:
The Euler Lagrange operator, for a trajectory `q : Time → X`,
and a lagrangian `Time → X → X → ℝ`, the Euler-Lagrange operator is
  `∂L/∂q - dₜ(∂L/∂(dₜ q))`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def eulerLagrangeOp (L : Time → X → X → ℝ) (q : Time → X) : Time → X

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.eulerLagrangeOp_eq
declarations.statement:
lemma eulerLagrangeOp_eq (L : Time → X → X → ℝ) (q : Time → X) :
    eulerLagrangeOp L q = fun t => gradient (L t · (∂ₜ q t)) (q t)
    - ∂ₜ (fun t' => gradient (L t' (q t') ·) (∂ₜ q t')) t

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.eulerLagrangeOp_zero
declarations.statement:
lemma eulerLagrangeOp_zero (q : Time → X) :
    eulerLagrangeOp (fun _ _ _ => 0) q = fun _ => 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.euler_lagrange_varGradient
declarations.doc:
The variational derivative of the action `∫ t, L t (q' t) (deriv q' t)` for a Lagrangian `L`
is equal to the `eulerLagrangeOp`.
declarations.statement:
theorem euler_lagrange_varGradient
    (L : Time → X → X → ℝ) (q : Time → X)
    (hq : ContDiff ℝ ∞ q) (hL : ContDiff ℝ ∞ ↿L) :
    (δ (q':=q), ∫ t, L t (q' t) (fderiv ℝ q' t 1)) = eulerLagrangeOp L q

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.canonicalMomentum
declarations.doc: The canonical momentum `∂L/∂q̇` of a curve `q`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def canonicalMomentum (q : ℝ → E) (τ : ℝ) : E →L[ℝ] ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.eulerLagrange
declarations.doc:
The Euler-Lagrange covector `∂L/∂q - dₜ(∂L/∂q̇)` of a curve `q`; the covector counterpart of
`eulerLagrangeOp`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def eulerLagrange (q : ℝ → E) (τ : ℝ) : E →L[ℝ] ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.contDiff_eulerLagrange
declarations.doc: The Euler-Lagrange covector of a smooth curve is smooth.
declarations.statement:
lemma contDiff_eulerLagrange {q : ℝ → E} (hq : ContDiff ℝ ∞ q) :
    ContDiff ℝ ∞ (eulerLagrange S t₀ q)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.eulerLagrange_congr
declarations.doc: The Euler-Lagrange covector at `τ` depends only on the germ of the curve at `τ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma eulerLagrange_congr {q g : ℝ → E} {τ : ℝ} (h : q =ᶠ[𝓝 τ] g) :
    eulerLagrange S t₀ q τ = eulerLagrange S t₀ g τ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.eulerLagrange_congr_lagrangian
declarations.doc: The Euler-Lagrange covector only depends on the Lagrangian near the curve.
declarations.statement:
lemma eulerLagrange_congr_lagrangian {S' : LagrangianSystem 𝓘(ℝ, E) ⟨E⟩} {q : ℝ → E} {τ : ℝ}
    {N : Set E} (hN : IsOpen N) (hq : ∀ᶠ σ in 𝓝 τ, q σ ∈ N)
    (h : ∀ p : ℝ × E × E, p.2.1 ∈ N → S.coord t₀ p = S'.coord t₀ p) :
    eulerLagrange S t₀ q τ = eulerLagrange S' t₀ q τ

modules.title: Forces
modules.doc:
This module defines forces acting on objects, expressed in a reference frame.
A `Force` records its target and its vector value over time. An `InternalForce`
additionally records a distinct source object.

The time-dependent vector describes the force acting on the target, without
prescribing how that force is determined. For example, a gravitational force can
be specified directly from the target's mass, while a constraint force can be
specified by its relation to the motion of the objects. Representing both by the
same type allows Newton's laws to be stated independently of the particular
interactions present.

The reference frame appears in the type of a force's vector values, keeping their
coordinate dependence explicit. The definition lives in the
`ClassicalMechanics.ReferenceFrame` namespace to support dot notation such as
`frame.Force Object`, but also occupies a general name that future non-particle
Newtonian formalizations may need.

The target type `Object` is therefore deliberately left arbitrary. Newtonian mechanics is
not limited to point particles, so this force representation is kept independent
of any particular model of matter, with the intention it may get generalized for
rigid body mechanics, continuum mechanics, or other Newtonian models in the future.

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.ReferenceFrame.Force
declarations.doc: A time-dependent force acting on an object.
declarations.statement:
structure Force (frame : ReferenceFrame d) (Object : Type) where
  /-- The force vector. -/
  value : ℝ → frame.Vector
  /-- The target object. -/
  target : Object
instance : CoeFun (frame.Force Object) (fun _ => ℝ → frame.Vector)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.ReferenceFrame.InternalForce
declarations.doc: A force between two objects.
declarations.statement:
structure InternalForce (frame : ReferenceFrame d) (Object : Type) extends frame.Force Object where
  /-- The source object. -/
  source : Object
  source_ne_target : source ≠ target
instance : CoeFun (frame.InternalForce Object) (fun _ => ℝ → frame.Vector)
instance : Coe (frame.InternalForce Object) (frame.Force Object)

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.ReferenceFrame.InternalForce.reverse
declarations.doc: The equal-and-opposite force with source and target exchanged.
declarations.statement: def InternalForce.reverse (force : frame.InternalForce Object) : frame.InternalForce Object

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.ReferenceFrame.netForce
declarations.doc: The net force on `object`.
declarations.statement:
def netForce (object : Object) (internalForces : Multiset (frame.InternalForce Object))
    (externalForces : Multiset (frame.Force Object)) (t : ℝ) : frame.Vector

modules.title: The Free Particle
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

The free particle is one of the simplest systems in classical mechanics: a particle of mass `m`
moving with no external forces acting on it. Physically, this means the particle just keeps moving
at constant velocity.

In this file, we work in a simple 1D coordinate system where position and velocity are functions
of time with values in `ℝ`. This keeps things easy to reason about. A more complete treatment would
use manifolds and tangent bundles.

## ii. Key results

The main things we show about the free particle are:

In the `Basic` module:
- `FreeParticle` stores the mass of the particle.
- `NewtonsSecondLaw` encodes the equation `m * q'' = 0`.
- `accel_zero` shows that this implies `q'' = 0`.
- `velocity_const_of_zero_acc` shows that zero acceleration means velocity is constant.
- `linearMomentum_conserved` shows that linear momentum stays constant over time.
- `kineticEnergy_conserved` shows that kinetic energy stays constant over time.

So overall, we formalise the usual chain:
Newton’s law → zero acceleration → constant velocity → constant momentum and energy.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The setup
- B. Equation of motion
  - B.1. Newton's second law
  - B.2. Zero acceleration
- C. What zero acceleration implies
  - C.1. Constant velocity
- D. Momentum
  - D.1. Linear momentum
  - D.2. Momentum conservation
- E. Energy
  - E.1. Kinetic energy
  - E.2. Energy conservation

## iv. References

* None.

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.FreeParticle
declarations.doc:
A classical free particle with positive mass.

A free particle is a mechanical system evolving in the absence of
external forces. The dynamics are therefore entirely determined by
Newton's second law with zero force.

The only parameter of the system is the particle mass. The assumption
that the mass is strictly positive is physically natural and is used
throughout the development when simplifying the equation of motion.
declarations.statement:
structure FreeParticle where
  /--
  The mass of the free particle.

  This parameter determines the inertial response of the particle in
  Newton's second law.
  -/
  mass : ℝ
  mass_pos : 0 < mass

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.FreeParticle.Trajectory
declarations.doc:
A trajectory is a time-dependent position function describing the motion
of the particle in one spatial dimension. Defining the trajectory.
declarations.statement: abbrev Trajectory

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.FreeParticle.velocity
declarations.doc:
The velocity of a trajectory at a given time.
This is defined as the time derivative of the position function.
declarations.statement: def velocity (s : FreeParticle) (q : Trajectory) (t : Time) : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.FreeParticle.linearMomentum
declarations.doc:
The linear momentum of the free particle along a trajectory.

This is given by the classical one-dimensional expression `p = m v`,
where `m` is the particle mass and `v` is the velocity.
declarations.statement: def linearMomentum (s : FreeParticle) (q : Trajectory) (t : Time) : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.FreeParticle.kineticEnergy
declarations.doc:
The kinetic energy of the free particle along a trajectory.

This is given by the classical expression `E = (1 / 2) m v²`,
where `m` is the particle mass and `v` is the velocity.
declarations.statement: def kineticEnergy (s : FreeParticle) (q : Trajectory) (t : Time) : ℝ

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.FreeParticle.NewtonsSecondLaw
declarations.doc:
Newton's second law for the free particle.

Since no external forces act on the particle, Newton's second law
reduces to the equation `m q'' = 0`, expressing that the acceleration
vanishes identically.
declarations.statement: def NewtonsSecondLaw (s : FreeParticle) (q : Trajectory) (t : Time) : Prop

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.FreeParticle.accel_zero
declarations.doc:
Newton's second law for a free particle implies that the acceleration
vanishes identically.

Since the particle mass is strictly positive, the equation
`m q'' = 0` can be simplified to `q'' = 0` by cancelling the mass
factor.
declarations.statement:
lemma accel_zero (s : FreeParticle) (q : Trajectory) (h : ∀ t, s.NewtonsSecondLaw q t) :
    ∀ t, deriv (deriv q) t = 0

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.FreeParticle.velocity_const_of_zero_acc
declarations.doc:
If the acceleration of a trajectory vanishes everywhere, then the
velocity is constant.

More precisely, if the second derivative of the trajectory is zero
for all times, then there exists a constant `v₀` such that the
velocity is equal to `v₀` at every time.

The second-order differentiability assumption is included to apply
standard results from real analysis relating vanishing derivatives to
constant functions.
declarations.statement:
lemma velocity_const_of_zero_acc (q : Time → ℝ) (h : ∀ t, deriv (deriv q) t = 0)
    (hcont : ContDiff ℝ 2 q) : ∃ v₀, ∀ t, deriv q t = v₀

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.FreeParticle.linearMomentum_conserved_of_velocity_const
declarations.doc: If a free-particle trajectory has constant velocity, then its linear momentum is constant.
declarations.statement:
lemma linearMomentum_conserved_of_velocity_const (s : FreeParticle) (q : Trajectory)
    (h : ∃ v₀, ∀ t, s.velocity q t = v₀) :
    ∃ p, ∀ t, s.linearMomentum q t = p

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.FreeParticle.linearMomentum_conserved
declarations.doc:
A free particle satisfying the equation of motion conserves linear momentum.

Newton's second law implies that the acceleration vanishes, so the velocity is constant.
Since the particle mass is fixed, the linear momentum is constant in time.
declarations.statement:
theorem linearMomentum_conserved (s : FreeParticle) (q : Trajectory)
    (h : ∀ t, s.NewtonsSecondLaw q t) (hcont : ContDiff ℝ 2 q) :
    ∃ p, ∀ t, s.linearMomentum q t = p

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.FreeParticle.kineticEnergy_conserved
declarations.doc:
A free particle satisfying the equation of motion conserves kinetic energy.

The proof follows the standard argument from classical mechanics:
Newton's second law implies that the acceleration vanishes, which in
turn implies that the velocity is constant. Since the kinetic energy
depends only on the square of the velocity, it follows that the kinetic
energy is constant in time.
declarations.statement:
theorem kineticEnergy_conserved (s : FreeParticle) (q : Trajectory)
    (h : ∀ t, s.NewtonsSecondLaw q t) (hcont : ContDiff ℝ 2 q) :
    ∃ E, ∀ t, s.kineticEnergy q t = E

modules.title: Hamilton's equations
modules.doc:
In this module, given a Hamiltonian function `H : Time → X → X → ℝ`,
we define the operator `hamiltonEqOp`
which when equals zero implies hamilton's equations.

We show that the variational derivative of the action functional
`∫ ⟪p, dq/dt⟫ - H(t, p, q) dt` is equal to the `hamiltonEqOp`
applied to `(p, q)`.

## References

* G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, "Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics", Section 3.1.2.
  <https://groups.csail.mit.edu/mac/users/gjs/6946/sicm-html/book-Z-H-36.html#%_sec_3.1.2>.
  [ref: sussman_wisdom_sicm]

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.hamiltonEqOp
declarations.doc:
Given a hamiltonian `H : Time → X → X → ℝ` the operator which when
set to zero implies the Hamilton equations.
declarations.statement:
noncomputable def hamiltonEqOp (H : Time → X → X → ℝ) (p : Time → X) (q : Time → X) :
    Time → X × X

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.hamiltonEqOp_eq
declarations.statement:
lemma hamiltonEqOp_eq (H : Time → X → X → ℝ) (p : Time → X) (q : Time → X) :
    hamiltonEqOp H p q = fun t => (∂ₜ q t + -gradient (fun x => H t x (q t)) (p t),
      - ∂ₜ p t + -gradient (fun x => H t (p t) x) (q t))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.hamiltonEqOp_eq_zero_iff_hamiltons_equations
declarations.statement:
lemma hamiltonEqOp_eq_zero_iff_hamiltons_equations (H : Time → X → X → ℝ)
    (p : Time → X) (q : Time → X) :
    hamiltonEqOp H p q = 0 ↔
    (∀ t, ∂ₜ q t = gradient (fun x => H t x (q t)) (p t)) ∧
    (∀ t, ∂ₜ p t = -gradient (fun x => H t (p t) x) (q t))

declarations.name: ClassicalMechanics.hamiltons_equations_varGradient
declarations.doc:
The variational derivative of `⟪(pq' t).1, ∂ₜ (Prod.snd ∘ pq') t⟫_ℝ - H t (pq' t).1 (pq' t).2`
for a hamiltonian `H` is equal to the Hamilton equations operator.
declarations.statement:
theorem hamiltons_equations_varGradient
    (H : Time → X → X → ℝ) (pq : Time → X × X) (hp : ContDiff ℝ ∞ pq)
    (hL : ContDiff ℝ ∞ ↿H) :
    (δ (pq':= pq), ∫ t, ⟪(pq' t).1, ∂ₜ (Prod.snd ∘ pq') t⟫_ℝ - H t (pq' t).1 (pq' t).2) =
    fun t => hamiltonEqOp H (fun t => (pq t).1) (fun t => (pq t).2) t

modules.title: The Poisson bracket
modules.doc:
The Poisson bracket of phase-space observables and their Hamiltonian time evolution.

## i. Overview

The Poisson bracket packages, into a single antisymmetric bilinear operation on phase-space
functions, the way an observable evolves along a Hamiltonian flow. Following the convention of
`hamiltonEqOp` in `HamiltonsEquations.lean`, a phase-space function is a function `f : X → X → ℝ`
read as `f p q` for `p` a momentum and `q` a position, both valued in a real inner product space
`X`. The bracket of two such functions is

$$\{f, g\} := \left\langle \frac{\partial f}{\partial q}, \frac{\partial g}{\partial p}
  \right\rangle - \left\langle \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}, \frac{\partial g}{\partial q}
  \right\rangle,$$

built from the same currying-and-`gradient` idiom `hamiltonEqOp` already uses to express partial
derivatives on phase space.

## ii. Key results

- `poissonBracket` : the Poisson bracket of two phase-space functions.
- `poissonBracket_eq_of_hasGradientAt` : computes the bracket from known partial gradients.
- `poissonBracket_antisymm` : the bracket is antisymmetric.
- `poissonBracket_self` : every observable Poisson-commutes with itself.
- `poissonBracket_add_left`, `poissonBracket_add_right`, `poissonBracket_const_mul_left`,
  `poissonBracket_const_mul_right` : the bracket is bilinear, that is additive and homogeneous in
  each argument.
- `poissonBracket_mul_left`, `poissonBracket_mul_right` : the bracket satisfies the Leibniz rule
  in each argument.
- `deriv_comp_eq_inner_gradient_add` : the time derivative of a phase-space function composed with
  a trajectory is the sum of its gradients paired with the trajectory's velocities.
- `deriv_comp_eq_poissonBracket` : along a solution of Hamilton's equations, the time derivative of
  an observable is its Poisson bracket with the Hamiltonian.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The definition of the Poisson bracket
- B. Antisymmetry
- C. Bilinearity
- D. The Leibniz rule
- E. Time evolution along a Hamiltonian flow
  - E.1. The chain rule for a phase-space function along a trajectory
  - E.2. Time evolution as the Poisson bracket with the Hamiltonian

## iv. References

* G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, "Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics", Section 3.2.
  <https://groups.csail.mit.edu/mac/users/gjs/6946/sicm-html/book-Z-H-37.html>.
  [ref: sussman_wisdom_sicm]

sections.text: ## A. The definition of the Poisson bracket
## B. Antisymmetry

## C. Bilinearity

The bracket is additive and homogeneous under scaling by a constant in each argument. We prove
this for the first argument; the second-argument versions follow from `poissonBracket_antisymm`.
## D. The Leibniz rule
